drop5:51

Man, please." 4 · how (the next move)Cut the "So, I just want to say thanks" line at 37:55 and hand directly to the shop-visit tease Dusty offers. 5 · rationaleNever signal the outro; the thanks beat releases viewers where the shop-visit tease would extend the session into the next video.

I spent the last 3 months attempting to build a massive Dungeons & Dragons gaming table for my client Dusty. And ever since I was a kid, I dreamed of playing Dungeons & Dragons. drop0:18
1 · what the curve showedThe opening 20 seconds shed roughly a quarter of arrivals (*6.4x the surrounding stop rate, 18,046 viewers, 100% down to 76.1%*). 2 · evidence at that second“settle it with a build competition” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The premise is stated, then restated across rules, stakes, and a tattoo callback before any building starts: "we're going to settle it with a build competition." 4 · how (the next move)Cut 0:26-0:34 rules recap and open cold on the 0:38 fire gag, then state the tattoo stake in one line. 5 · rationaleIntro loss ran +5.4pp over the channel median here; the premise the thumbnail already sold is being explained instead of delivered.
drop5:12
1 · what the curve showedThe post-fire cleanup beat loses viewers at the channel's normal rate for this position (*6.0x local spike, 2,255 viewers, 47.4% down to 44.4%*). 2 · evidence at that second“I still got a little bit of work to do” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The fire gag pays off, then 90 seconds of self-explanation and cleanup follow: "I still got a little bit of work to do." 4 · how (the next move)Cut 5:22-6:32 cleanup narration and jump from the fire reaction directly to the day-two lumber run. 5 · rationaleRetention drops the moment tension is spent; the flame-jacket joke resolves and nothing new arrives for 90 seconds.
drop7:48
1 · what the curve showedThe outfeed-table bit loses viewers at below the channel norm for this position (*3.8x local spike, 886 viewers, 44.5% down to 43.4%*). 2 · evidence at that second“one that you're using?” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A back-and-forth over shared shop space plays out in repeated one-liners: "one that you're using?" 4 · how (the next move)Cut 7:56-8:06 repeated "one that you're using" beats down to two exchanges and land on "Can I cut this one thing?" 5 · rationaleKill all repetition — verbal, visual, narrative; the gag lands on the first ask and flattens on the fourth.
drop12:01

peak24:22

1 · what the curve showedThe wide-belt-sander detour loses viewers at well below the channel norm for this position (*9.2x local spike, 1,354 viewers, 39.0% down to 37.7%*). 2 · evidence at that second“run this through a wide belt sander” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The final-day push pauses to explain an off-site fix: "we found someone on a Sunday that can run this through a wide belt sander." 4 · how (the next move)Cut 27:19-27:35 flatness explanation and jump from the paint problem straight to the sander in action. 5 · rationaleThe moment held better than the channel typically does here, so tighten rather than restructure — compress the teardown phase.
peak28:55

peak30:13
1 · what the curve showedThe finished-piece reveal pulls viewers back and holds six samples (*audience rose 2.0%, 917 viewers regained, 39.6% present*). 2 · evidence at that second“final coat finished on here” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The build closes on visible finish work: "I got the final coat finished on here. I got the touch-ups done on the legs." 4 · how (the next move)Hold the finished table off-frame here and cut to the judging walk-up, revealing both tables only at 31:05. 5 · rationaleWithhold the finished thing so the reveal keeps pulling; showing the table before the judge spends the payoff early.
peak30:52
1 · what the curve showedThe judge arrival pulls viewers back to watch (*audience rose 4.4%, 2,019 viewers regained, 41.3% present*). 2 · evidence at that second“He showed up wearing a blazer” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The verdict setup lands with a named outside judge: "This is my buddy Scott Pope. He showed up wearing a blazer to judge this competition." 4 · how (the next move)Tease Scott Pope's arrival at the 0:38 cold open so first-time viewers know a judge decides, and hold the winner past 32:00. 5 · rationaleDopamine spikes at the announcement of a reward — front-loading the judge as the announced payoff pulls more viewers through the middle to this peak.

The One Mistake That Could Cost You $12,000

drop0:27

drop0:12
1 · what the curve showedThe opening loses roughly a quarter of the room in twelve seconds (*10.2x the surrounding stop rate, 106,773 viewers, 97.7% down to 74.9%*). 2 · evidence at that second“real quick before I get started” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The video opens on personal life admin before the premise — a new baby, a shop break-in, a slab delay — with the words "real quick before I get started." 4 · how (the next move)Cut 0:00-0:19 and open on 0:20 "my friend John Malecki did a shark table carving" over the rattlesnake reference image. 5 · rationaleIntros must deliver the thumbnail promise in seconds; front-loaded personal exposition before any carving footage wastes the first 30 seconds where 30% typically leaves.
drop4:15
1 · what the curve showedA 46-second stretch mid-milling sheds viewers well above the local norm (*6.5x surrounding stop rate, 1.6x channel norm, 18,161 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“gently tap the Subscribe button” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The carving pauses for a subscribe ask layered over glue-drying and scrap-sorting — "gently tap the Subscribe button" — with no new information on screen. 4 · how (the next move)Cut the subscribe ask at 4:23-4:40 and rejoin on 4:40 "before I start carving I need to get on my computer," moving the CTA to the end screen. 5 · rationalePacing is the flow of NEW information every ~5 seconds; a mid-video CTA over a stripping-down phase stacks two known retention losers.
drop9:04
1 · what the curve showedRetention collapses at the sponsor handoff mid-carve (*12.9x surrounding stop rate, 5.9x the channel's norm here, 24,028 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“tell you all about this jackery power station” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A straight Jackery read opens cold on "take a quick second here to tell you all about this jackery power station," halting the carving story to pitch the product. 4 · how (the next move)Cross-cut the read against the burr shaping shots from 9:16-10:15, and rewrite the first line to open on portable shop power, not the brand name. 5 · rationaleStraight reads cost 10-20% of the room; cross-cutting with the progressing story cuts that to ~2%, and ads must never open with "sponsored by." cautionJackery is a paid sponsor with contracted talking points; confirm the rewrite and visual treatment with the brand before shipping.
peak10:25

peak10:37
1 · what the curve showedA second climb lands as the fix is announced and holds 44 samples (*+5.4% of viewers present, 9,390 regained, 35.6% audience*). 2 · evidence at that second“glue on a new block” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The plan to recover the mistake is stated plainly — "sand all of this lower jaw off and then glue on a new block" — with visible confidence about the fix. 4 · how (the next move)Tease this recovery at 9:04 before the sponsor ("the jaw's about to go wrong — fix coming") so anticipation carries through the read. 5 · rationaleAds hold best at the height of anticipation, not after a payoff; seeding the jaw fix pre-ad converts the sponsor into a suspense bridge.
peak18:43
1 · what the curve showedThe audience jumps back near the finish and the video ends ranked 14 of 139 (*+8.4% of viewers present, 17,119 regained, 42.4% still watching*). 2 · evidence at that second“looks like what prison food tastes like” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The self-roast escalates into a rapid-fire list — "looks like what prison food tastes like," Helen Keller, chimpanzee, Abraham Lincoln, JFK, Springsteen — that viewers scrub back to catch. 4 · how (the next move)Tease this roast in the first 30 seconds as a cold-open cutaway ("my newborn infant daughter even told me it sucks") before cutting to the rattlesnake reference. 5 · rationaleFront-loading the video's proven emotional peak gives the intro an out-of-context hook and pays off the packaging promise immediately.

drop0:12

drop9:51

peak11:21

drop16:29

drop0:10
1 · what the curve showedThe opening 12 seconds shed viewers, but softer than this channel's usual intro (*7.95% stop rate, 0.8x the channel norm, 12,444 viewers lost*). 2 · evidence at that second“no idea what we're even gonna build” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Standard on-camera greeting and premise setup — "I have no idea what we're even gonna build" — delays any visible hook or stakes. 4 · how (the next move)Keep the current open; test front-loading a 3-second cut of the finished cabinet reveal from 17:44 before "so I just showed up in Chicago". 5 · rationaleIntro loss (14.5%) already beats the channel's 22.9% average for intros, so protect the win and only trial upside toward the 0% best-in-cohort. cautionThe cold open may spoil the reveal viewers rewind to at 6:10 — pull the test if the 6:10 replay peak shrinks.
peak6:10
1 · what the curve showedAudience climbs and holds for 40 samples as the design is shown and the slab becomes the cabinet doors (*+4.3% of viewers present, 2,028 regained, 67th percentile vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“act as the doors of the cabinet” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind to see the design approval and the first cut into the live-edge slab — "this Live Edge slab is going to act as the doors of the cabinet". 4 · how (the next move)Tease this door-slab moment in the first 20 seconds with a locked-off shot of the slab, without revealing it becomes the doors. 5 · rationaleA reveal that earns rewinds is an asset — structure toward it by teasing early and withholding the finished object.
peak6:44
1 · what the curve showedA brief rise on the day-one wrap montage right before the wake-up cut (*+2.2% of viewers present, 1,062 regained, 71st percentile vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“we called it a night on day one” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind the end-of-day-one recap — "after a long day of traveling designing going to pick up materials and working we called it a night" — that summarises the day's progress. 4 · how (the next move)Add an on-screen day-counter graphic at 6:45 and reuse it at every day break, so the progression is visible when viewers scrub back. 5 · rationaleProgress trackers and on-screen timers hold retention, and reminding viewers of structure every ~2 minutes reinforces the day-by-day spine.
drop6:55
1 · what the curve showedA 22-second segue between day one and day two loses a small amount, in line with the channel's baseline here (*0.83% stop rate, 1.1x the channel norm, 1,690 viewers lost*). 2 · evidence at that second“it's day two let's go” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A time-jump handoff with a wake-up gag — "hey Mr Bill it's wake up it's time to get to work it's day two" — followed by an epoxy-cure explainer before any new action. 4 · how (the next move)Tighten 6:45-7:07 by cutting the wake-up bit and opening day two on the epoxy pour itself, keeping the "feeling the squeeze" line as voiceover. 5 · rationalePacing is the flow of new information; compressing the transition keeps something changing every ~5 seconds through the day-break.
peak11:36
1 · what the curve showedA one-sample tick up as the epoxy piece is demolded on day four (*+3.1% of viewers present, 1,464 regained, 65th percentile vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“pull these right off” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers scrub back to the demold reveal — "we're gonna de-mold this thing... pull these right off" — after the schedule-pressure beat lands. 4 · how (the next move)Add a 20-second riser starting at 11:16 under "we're running behind schedule" and hold silence on the screw-pull at 11:51. 5 · rationaleAnticipatory audio ~20 seconds before a key moment flattens retention through the buildup and holds more of the room to the payoff. cautionOne-sample ticks can be data artifacts — treat this as a secondary confirmation of the 6:10 peak, not a standalone finding.
drop17:57

1 · what the curve showedThe Jeff bit lost 7.8 points across 30 seconds at the 18% mark (*14.8x spike, 169,056 viewers, 3.3x channel norm, 55% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“Thou shalt not lay stain upon thy Live Edge wood” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A scripted mock-scripture skit — 'the third commandment in the book of Desta is Thou shalt not lay stain upon thy Live Edge wood' — stalls the build with no new information. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 4:10-4:34 and rejoin on 'I say stain it black so black it is', keeping only the decision and the first shot of stain going on. 5 · rationalePacing is flow of new information; the skit repeats a decision the viewer already accepts and 14.8x the surrounding stop rate shows they check out.
drop11:09
1 · what the curve showedThe Growatt sponsor read cost 8.8 points of the remaining room in 30 seconds (*7.9x spike, 172,820 viewers, 7.6x channel norm, 39% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“thanks to the sponsor of this video growatt” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A straight ad opens cold on 'thanks to the sponsor of this video growatt' right after the ice-storm anecdote, with no story cross-cut. 4 · how (the next move)Cut back to the epoxy pour progressing on screen while the read runs, and open the read on the Oklahoma power-loss stake, not the brand name. 5 · rationaleCross-cutting a read against the live build cuts sponsor loss from 10-20% to roughly 2%, and this read is bleeding 8.8 points against a 0.64% norm. cautionConfirm Growatt's contract allows reordering the first line and running the read over B-roll; if locked, keep copy but move the read earlier while the flood-coat outcome is still unresolved.
peak12:38
1 · what the curve showedAudience climbed 6.7 points and held 45 samples as the epoxy pour went wrong (*63,310 viewers regained, 58% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“it all went to hell” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewound to see the failure land — 'it all went to hell' and 'we have a bit of a problem' — and the diagnosis of epoxy flowing over the center. 4 · how (the next move)Tease this failure in the first 30 seconds alongside the crack, so newcomers know a second disaster is coming and stay through the sponsor to reach it. 5 · rationaleA reveal that earns rewinds is an asset — surfacing it in the opening keeps the mid-video valley from bleeding out before viewers reach the payoff.
peak15:07
1 · what the curve showedAudience rose 2.5 points for 5 samples on the future-Johnny cut-in (*23,997 viewers regained, 61% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“hey future Johnny here” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A time-jump confession lands — 'hey future Johnny here it's been a little over a month since I've last touched this table' — and viewers rewind for the reset. 4 · how (the next move)Move a shorter version of this beat before the 11:09 sponsor read as a suspense layer so viewers know the table is stalled before the ad hits. 5 · rationalePlacing live suspense in front of the ad follows the rule that reads hold when anticipation is live, not after a payoff.
peak18:20
1 · what the curve showedAudience rose 2.1 points for 4 samples as the gold leaf reveal landed (*20,678 viewers regained, 66% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“this is the result that I was wanting” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The kintsugi payoff finally shows — 'this is the result that I was wanting' with the gold bleeding into the black epoxy — and viewers rewind the reveal. 4 · how (the next move)Hold on the finished gold-leaf shot two seconds longer with music stripped, and cut the next 'now I can fully penetrate this slab' line back by a beat. 5 · rationaleStretching a conflict-resolved beat with bare sound holds the room, and this is the video's strongest reveal against similar videos at 66%.

drop0:09

drop0:10
1 · what the curve showedThe opening ten seconds hold 137 of 138 other uploads, then normalise to the channel's usual intro loss (*11.57% stop rate, 14,073 viewers, 0.9x channel intro average*). 2 · evidence at that second“transforming it into this painted white stone fireplace” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The cold open shows the finished white fireplace with the 300-pound beam already installed, releasing the outcome the thumbnail sold before any journey begins. 4 · how (the next move)Test recutting 0:15-0:26 to open on the chainsaw work or the beam being wrestled into place, keeping the finished reveal for the payoff. 5 · rationaleIf the outcome is visible in the thumbnail, the intro must sell the journey and obstacles, not the outcome (Joos). cautionVerify the finished-fireplace shot is not doing thumbnail-promise duty; if it is, keep a 1-second glimpse and revert if 0:30 retention drops below the current 80.5%.
drop8:00
1 · what the curve showedA cold pivot from mantel selection into an Anker sponsor read costs nearly a third of the room (*6.27% stop rate, 9.8x channel norm, 7,040 viewers lost*). 2 · evidence at that second“today i'm showing off the anker 521” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The read opens with brand-first ad language mid-decision about the beam, releasing the live question of whether the piece fits. 4 · how (the next move)Rewrite 7:56-8:10 so the first sentence ties power outages to shop work, and cross-cut the read with continuing beam-prep footage rather than cutting away. 5 · rationaleA straight one-minute read costs 10-20% of remaining audience; cross-cutting the read with the progressing story cuts that to ~2% (Joos), and no read should open on "this video is sponsored by". cautionAnker likely has script-approval rights; negotiate the opening sentence and B-roll treatment with the brand before recutting.

peak9:41

peak9:51
1 · what the curve showedA third replay clusters on the stated build plan, holding 38 samples (*9.3% rise, 2,291 viewers regained, 80th percentile*). 2 · evidence at that second“logistical and structural challenges of actually mounting” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The rewind lands on the concrete task list — sand the driftwood tone off, stain darker, then solve the mounting problem on a 300-pound beam. 4 · how (the next move)Add an on-screen progress tracker at 9:34 listing chainsaw / sand / stain / mount, and tick items as each is completed through 15:00. 5 · rationaleProgress trackers and reminders of the goal every ~2 minutes hold retention through the middle (Joos).
drop15:31
1 · what the curve showedThe wrap-up sheds a third of remaining viewers, running 1.3x the channel's own outro average and beating only the bottom of the outro cohort (*2.21% stop rate, 5,640 viewers, 35.4% loss vs 27.0% channel outro average*). 2 · evidence at that second“popped right on with just a little bit of persuasion” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The install is narrated in past tense as already finished before viewers see it happen: mounting, washers and finish are summarised in one breath. 4 · how (the next move)Rebuild 15:02-15:29 the way "I Built the Table of My Dreams" ends at 35:51: hold the mount attempt in real time with sound stripped, then cut on the beam locking in. 5 · rationaleRetention drops the moment viewers sense the video is ending — resolve at the emotional high and break off within seconds, never narrate past the payoff (Joos, Cannell).

1 · what the curve showedThe sponsor read collapses the room from 54.4% to 34.3% in sixteen seconds (*61.0x the surrounding stop rate, 13.3x the channel norm, 28,298 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“talk about the sponsor of this video” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A cold hand-off from build to ad opens on "talk about the sponsor of this video," then pitches M1 as a "super app that puts you in control of your wealth." 4 · how (the next move)Cut 3:54-4:16 and cross-cut the M1 read over the brad-nail glue-up and caster install, opening on "invest, borrow, save." 5 · rationaleA straight one-minute read costs 10-20% of the room; cross-cutting the read with progressing build footage drops that to roughly 2%. cautionVerify M1's contract allows re-cut voiceover over B-roll and a rewritten opening line before shipping the edit.
peak4:55

peak5:03

peak5:11

1 · what the curve showedThe finish step bleeds 2,938 viewers across 38 seconds (*7.0x spike, 1.6x the channel's norm here, 23rd percentile vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“use my discount that i've got linked” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Tension is spent — the honed marble is already shown at 7:40 — and the segment turns into wax application before a sponsor handoff at 8:31 to "total boat... use my discount." 4 · how (the next move)Cut 8:02-8:27 wax explanation, move the totalboat read to 4:11 during the "three and a half minutes" timer, and end at 8:30 on the finished top. 5 · rationaleRetention drops the moment viewers sense the video is ending; ads placed while suspense is live (the epoxy curing) cost ~2% vs 10-20% for straight reads after a payoff. cautionThe totalboat placement may be contractually anchored to the outro — if the brand won't move it, keep it there but cap total post-reveal runtime at 15 seconds.

1 · what the curve showedA nine-second window loses roughly one in six viewers still watching (*3.93% stop rate, 30.8x the surrounding rate, 9,857 viewers*), against a channel norm of 0.70%. 2 · evidence at that second“plastic tubing... medical tubing and a syringe” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Static epoxy prep with no visible progress: 'plastic tubing... medical tubing and a syringe... pull the epoxy up through the pins'. 4 · how (the next move)Compress 6:00-6:35 to a 6-second montage over music and cut straight to the tempered blade reveal at 6:42. 5 · rationaleStripping-down phases before a build lose people — compress them and keep new information landing every ~5 seconds (Joos).
drop7:58
1 · what the curve showedA 28-second window drops the room from 47.8% to 41.8% (*3.40% stop rate, 18.0x the surrounding rate, 7,213 viewers*), five times the channel's norm here. 2 · evidence at that second“get your first audiobook for free” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A straight Audible read that opens on the ask: 'my viewers can get your first audiobook for free plus two audible originals'. 4 · how (the next move)Cross-cut the 7:54-8:16 read against the five-hour bevel grind footage, and open the read on the audiobook, not the offer. 5 · rationaleCross-cutting a read with the progressing story drops ad loss from 10-20% to ~2%; never open with the sign-up ask (Joos). cautionConfirm Audible's contract permits reordering the first line and running the read over B-roll; if locked, trial the cross-cut on the back half only.
peak9:21
1 · what the curve showedThe audience rose 2.9% and held for 29 samples immediately after the sponsor ends (*1,234 viewers regained, 42.7% present*). 2 · evidence at that second“all the way to a thousand grit” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers scrubbed back to the polish-and-grind work: 'work my way up through the grits all the way to a thousand grit'. 4 · how (the next move)Extend the 9:00-9:30 polishing sequence by 10 seconds and add on-screen grit callouts (400, 800, 1000, 3000). 5 · rationaleA reveal that earns rewinds is an asset — tease it earlier and structure toward it (Hayden; 7 Editing Tips).
peak13:01

peak13:10

peak6:33

drop0:04
1 · what the curve showedThe opening beat sheds 15 points before Johnny finishes his first sentence (*58.6x spike, 1,338 viewers, 99.8% to 84.7%*). 2 · evidence at that second“welcome back to Johnny builds” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The video greets the channel and restates the thumbnail's premise instead of paying it off: "welcome back to Johnny builds and today I'm building this geometric wall art clock". 4 · how (the next move)Cut 0:07-0:14 and open cold on the ripping shot at 0:24 with a one-line stake over it. 5 · rationaleIntros exist to deliver context and stakes fast; a greeting plus premise-restatement is the exact opener Joos flags as guaranteed loss.
drop3:48

peak5:50

drop6:14

2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:06
1 · what the curve showedThe opening bleeds nearly two viewers in five before the first cut is made (*39.2% lost, 1.7x the channel's intro average, 14,093 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“welcome back to Johnny builds today” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The video greets and restates the thumbnail before any hook: "welcome back to Johnny builds today I am building this reading nook bench." 4 · how (the next move)Rebuild this open the way "I Built the Table of My Dreams" does at 0:00, which lost 0.0% — drop the greeting and open on the finished nook with the daughter in it. 5 · rationale0:30 holds only 61.7% versus a 73.2% channel median, so the intro is 11.5pp below the creator's own norm and needs the channel's proven pattern.
drop3:09
1 · what the curve showedA quiet dado-and-pocket-hole passage loses viewers at 4.5x the surrounding rate across 24 seconds (*820 viewers, 36.9% down to 35.5%*). 2 · evidence at that second“these will be hidden on the backside” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The segment repeats a joinery beat already shown, narrated flatly: "here I added pocket holes to the center support and all of these will be hidden." 4 · how (the next move)Merge 3:09-3:32 with the earlier dado shot into one 8-second joinery block and cross-cut it with the spacer-block glue-up. 5 · rationaleKill visual and verbal repetition — a second hidden-joinery beat teaches viewers nothing new and the chart flattens then drops on schedule.
drop4:43
1 · what the curve showedA 24-second stretch mid-build sheds viewers at 3.8x the surrounding rate as assembly repeats itself (*973 viewers, 34.1% down to 32.0%*). 2 · evidence at that second“jumping up there and trying it out” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Three near-identical assembly beats stack with no new information: "drove in all the remaining pocket screws" then the creator "jumping up there and trying it out." 4 · how (the next move)Cut 4:43-5:07 down to a five-second montage ending on the sit-test, then hard-cut to the maple face-frame milling. 5 · rationalePacing is the flow of NEW information; three consecutive pocket-screw beats break the every-five-seconds change rule and the audience leaves on cue.
peak8:10
1 · what the curve showedA brief rise as the finish goes on and the timeline is stated (*+1.3%, 334 viewers regained, 63% vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“took about two three hours” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The creator names the payoff timeframe out loud: "whole finished process took about two three hours and look great." 4 · how (the next move)Front-load this "two to three hours" line as an on-screen timer at 0:25 so the whole build reads against a live countdown. 5 · rationaleProgress trackers and on-screen timers hold retention; the audience is already rewinding to hear the duration, so promise it upfront.
peak8:45
1 · what the curve showedAudience climbs and holds for nine samples as the screw-hiding trick is shown (*+2.3%, 560 viewers regained, 55% vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“tabs out of some leftover maple” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind to the small problem-solve: "made these tabs out of some leftover maple to hide the screw heads." 4 · how (the next move)Tease this maple-tab fix at 0:20 with a two-second shot of the finished tab, promising the trick before the build begins. 5 · rationaleA reveal that earns rewinds is an asset — surfacing it in the intro closes the interest gap that the current greeting-only open leaves wide.
peak9:32
1 · what the curve showedA small rise as the finished nook is named and the daughter is mentioned (*+1.2%, 301 viewers regained, 45% vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“my daughter was a huge fan” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The emotional payoff finally lands in words: "my daughter was a huge fan." 4 · how (the next move)Cut everything after 9:38 — the thumbs-up and subscribe pitch — and end on the daughter shot with a two-second end-screen card. 5 · rationaleRetention drops the moment viewers sense the outro; ending on the emotional high instead of the plug protects session watch time. cautionConfirm the daughter appears on camera here; if not, hold on the finished nook wide shot and keep the "huge fan" line as voiceover.

2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:05
1 · what the curve showedThe opening seven seconds bleed nearly half the room, running double the channel's own intro loss (*8.9x spike, 23,508 viewers, 47.4% intro loss vs 22.9% channel average*). 2 · evidence at that second“welcome to my new channel johnnie builds” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The video opens on unrelated honeybee narration before pivoting to a channel welcome and premise restate: "welcome to my new channel johnnie builds". 4 · how (the next move)Cut 0:00-0:19 entirely and open on the welding sparks around 1:47, the way "I Built the Table of My Dreams" opens cold at 0:00 with 0.0% loss. 5 · rationaleIntros must deliver title-promise context and stakes in two sentences, never a logo sting or self-introduction — the honeybee cold-open is doing neither.
peak1:40
1 · what the curve showedThe audience rises into the first welding attempt, well above similar videos at this position (*2.1% present regained, 1,025 viewers, 61st percentile vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“then it was my turn to give it a go” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind to the moment the creator first strikes an arc: "greg has shown me how to tack weld each section together and then it was my turn". 4 · how (the next move)Front-load a 2-second flash of the first weld attempt into the opening 10 seconds as the cold-open hook replacing the honeybee narration. 5 · rationaleOpening on a strong-emotion moment forces "wait, what's happening?" — the first-weld beat is already earning rewinds, which makes it the video's proven interest asset.
drop1:46
1 · what the curve showedA 39-second stretch loses 2,158 viewers even though the per-second stop rate matches the channel norm (*9.4x spike, 1.0x vs channel, 56th percentile vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“this is actually my first time welding” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The creator pauses the build to narrate a personal learning aside: "this is actually my first time welding" followed by "I still have a ton to learn". 4 · how (the next move)Trim 1:56-2:08 and cross-cut the "first time welding" admission over Greg's tack-weld demo, so the aside runs under progressing action instead of pausing it. 5 · rationaleRetention editing keeps cuts fast until conflict, then holds — a static self-assessment aside with no visible progression is exactly the kind of beat that flattens pacing.
drop3:15

peak8:21
1 · what the curve showedThe audience climbs back and holds through the finish application, the strongest rewind on the video (*4.1% of viewers present, 1,470 regained, held 8 samples*). 2 · evidence at that second“deep Browns and tans of the walnut jump out” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers scrub back to the Danish oil going on the walnut top: "I just love how the deep Browns and tans of the walnut jump out when the finish is applied". 4 · how (the next move)Tease this finish reveal in the first 30 seconds with a two-frame flash of the oiled walnut, then withhold it until 8:21 so the promise pulls viewers through the build. 5 · rationaleA reveal that earns rewinds is an asset — dopamine spikes on the announcement, so teasing it early converts the same moment into an intro hook and a payoff.
peak8:32
1 · what the curve showedA second rewind lands eleven seconds later on the same finish sequence (*3.4% of viewers present, 1,286 regained, held 6 samples*). 2 · evidence at that second“this has to be my favorite part of the build” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The narration explicitly names the moment as the emotional peak of the build: "this has to be my favorite part of the build". 4 · how (the next move)Stretch 8:31-8:41 by 3-4 seconds of bare-sound b-roll of the oil soaking in, and add a riser starting around 8:15 to flatten retention into the peak. 5 · rationaleRisers ~20 seconds before a key moment hold up to 10% more of the room, and stretching a payoff with music stripped keeps retention stable while extending screen time.
